title: Distinguishing vigilance decrement and low task demands from mind-wandering: A machine learning analysis of EEG.
summary: Across-task EEG classification found mind-wandering was separable from low vigilance and low task demand; the self-report-trained classifier predicted mind-wandering while classifiers trained on vigilance or task-demand labels did not, with source-localized features differing among states. Thirty participants; 10-fold and leave-one-participant-out cross-validation plus across-task testing against intermittent self-reports. Exploratory evidence with limited sample size and self-report labels.
ai_technology: SVM classifiers use EEG features to test whether mind-wandering shares neural patterns with low vigilance or low task demand; dipole fitting localizes significant classifier features.

source_review.scope: Read the primary article’s Methods and Results. SVM classifiers trained on EEG from 30 participants distinguished conditions of vigilance and task demand and were tested across tasks against probe-reported mind-wandering. The vigilance- and task-demand-trained classifiers did not predict mind-wandering above chance, whereas the self-report-trained classifier did; source localization associated the states with distinct neural correlates. PubMed and the primary paper identify electronic publication on 2020-06-28; a targeted title/DOI search found no earlier preprint/version. Searches of both supplied active and archived snapshots found no same mind-wandering result. The result is exploratory: small sample, self-report labels, and source-localization interpretation.
